analysis.one_liner: Allows union contracts nationwide to require workers to pay union fees, overriding state right-to-work laws.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it was referred to the Senate HELP Committee and died there when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal labor law currently lets states pass "right-to-work" laws that bar union contracts from requiring workers to pay union dues or fees. About half the states have such laws. This bill would repeal that permission, so unions everywhere could negotiate contracts requiring workers they represent to contribute to the cost of that representation. The bill never got a hearing or vote; it died in the Senate committee it was referred to.
analysis.who_benefits: Labor unions and the workers they represent. Unions could collect fees from all workers covered by their contracts, including in the roughly half of states with right-to-work laws, giving them more resources to bargain over wages and working conditions. Workers who want union representation would benefit from better-resourced unions; no worker would be forced to join a union, only potentially required to pay fees for representation they receive.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Unions and the workers they represent

how_it_helps.text: Repealing NLRA Section 14(b) would remove the federal authorization for state laws that ban union security agreements, letting union contracts require fee payment in every state.
Unions in right-to-work states could collect fees from the workers they represent, strengthening their finances and bargaining position in those states.

analysis.who_pays: Nonmember workers in right-to-work states who would have to pay union fees as a condition of employment under union contracts, and employers who would face stronger union bargaining. Workers who prefer to work for free of any union payment requirement would bear a direct cost.

drawbacks.text: The bill would override state right-to-work laws that voters and legislatures in more than half the states have adopted, taking that decision away from states.
Requiring nonmembers to pay union fees is the bill's central change, and it would raise the cost of taking a unionized job for workers who would prefer not to pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Union membership and dues are voluntary even under this bill — no one could be forced to join a union, only required to pay for representation a union is legally obligated to provide. The chief drawback is that repeal would shift choices about union security from state legislatures to federal law, which critics in right-to-work states would call an override of state policy. The bill also died without any committee action, so its actual costs were never litigated in a hearing record.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 8, 2022, near the end of the 117th Congress, with 19 Senate sponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day, and no further action was ever taken.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired without a committee vote, a floor vote, or any hearing in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and anti-union groups who defend state right-to-work laws benefit, since union security agreements remain banned in those states. Workers in right-to-work states who prefer not to pay union fees also keep the status quo.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led 18 cosponsors.

for.name: Bernie Sanders and other cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including 17 of 48 Senate Democrats and the chamber's other independent.

against.name: Business and anti-union advocacy groups
against.what_they_did: Long-standing opposition to repealing state right-to-work laws shaped the environment in which no committee action was taken.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no markup, vote, or hearing appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors were Democrats or the chamber's independents aligned with Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and with 50 Republicans holding committee and floor leverage, it went nowhere.

industries.note: The bill would let unions collect fees from all workers they represent, including in the roughly half of states with right-to-work laws, boosting union membership and revenue. For workers, this means stronger unions negotiating pay and conditions, though some would owe fees they do not pay today.
Employers could no longer rely on state right-to-work laws to keep unions from requiring fee payment, which unions argue raises labor costs and employers argue preserves worker flexibility.
